I'm Raja, a CS undergrad & AI Intern skilled in Python, C++, Java, and backend architecture. Team NextNova is tackling "Create Health Monitoring Software" to build a fail-safe medical dashboard that tracks astronaut vitals in deep space.

Since I'm handling the backend, data, and AI/prompt engineering, I need:

Frontend Devs (React/JS) for the UI

UI/UX Designers for a sleek space-themed layout

Data Visualizers (Chart.js) for real-time graphs
summary:
ASTRA (Astronaut Health Monitoring & Risk Assessment System) is a mission-aware, web-based health-monitoring prototype that helps astronauts assess their own health during long-duration missions. We designed an 11-screen platform covering vital signs (heart rate, SpO2, temperature, respiratory rate, blood pressure), mental well-being check-ins, exercise and recovery, daily routines, an interactive 3D human body map, explainable risk flags, an alert center, and exportable health reports. One shared platform adapts to three environments: Spacecraft/Transit, Lunar Surface, and Mars Surface.

ASTRA addresses the challenge by collecting health indicators, comparing them against each astronaut’s personal baseline, and presenting clear, explainable next steps, including when to contact a flight surgeon. It targets NASA’s Human Research Program hazards such as radiation, isolation, and altered gravity, and works offline-first to handle communication delays with Earth.

This matters because on Artemis and Mars missions, astronauts must act as their own first responders. ASTRA supports early detection and informed action while staying honest about its limits: it is a prototype using synthetic data, not a diagnostic or clinically validated medical device.
details:
ASTRA: Project Details

What it does and how it works

ASTRA is a web-based health-monitoring prototype for astronauts on long-duration missions. The astronaut starts by choosing an environment (Spacecraft/Transit, Lunar Surface, or Mars Surface), which loads the matching risk categories, routines, and context labels.

Data then moves through seven steps:

  1. Collect: readings come from manual entry, supported devices, or a clearly labelled simulator.
  2. Validate: units, timestamps, and sources are checked.
  3. Store: the original record is saved with its provenance.
  4. Analyse: values are compared with the astronaut’s personal baseline and recent trends.
  5. Contextualise: the selected environment and mission phase are applied.
  6. Respond: the system creates an explainable flag or recommendation.
  7. Display: results appear on the dashboard, in alerts, history, and reports.

The 11 screens cover environment setup, a mission dashboard, an interactive body map, vital signs, mental well-being, risk assessment, exercise and recovery, a daily routine, an alert and action center, history and reports, and settings. Every value shows its source, timestamp, unit, and quality (measured, manual, derived, or simulated).

Benefits

  • Astronauts get early, understandable warnings instead of raw numbers.
  • Alerts explain what changed and which records caused them, so there is no opaque “health score.”
  • It works offline-first, so entry and rule checks continue during communication delays.
  • Flight surgeons receive structured, traceable reports.
  • One shared platform avoids building three separate apps.

Intended impact

ASTRA aims to support autonomous self-assessment on Artemis and future Mars missions, where astronauts are their own first responders. It targets NASA Human Research Program hazards such as radiation, isolation, altered gravity, and distance from Earth. Its logic could later extend to Earth telemedicine for remote areas.

Tools and technologies

  • Frontend — React 19, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS.
  • Ingestion & Validation — Wearable readings ingested through the Node.js API; request data is handled and validated in TypeScript.
  • 3D Health Views — Three.js for interactive anatomy, with GLB models.
  • Backend — A custom Node.js HTTP API written in TypeScript.
  • Data Storage — Local SQLite using Node’s built-in node:sqlite module.
  • Authentication & Roles — Custom login and session handling, with astronaut, flight surgeon, and medical staff roles.
  • Health Monitoring — Vital signs and wearable readings, symptom and body assessments, mental wellbeing check-ins, and environmental hazard telemetry.
  • Risk & Medical Guidance — A rule-based risk engine, alerts, and reviewed medical guidance.
  • Analytics & Reports — Backend analytics and mission reports with CSV, JSON, and Markdown formats.
  • Version Control — Git; GitHub.

No specialised hardware was required. Device integration (Bluetooth Low Energy and device SDKs) is planned only for supported hardware, and the prototype uses manual and simulated data.

Creativity

  • Environment-aware configuration changes risk categories, routines, and recommendations, not just the background image.
  • The clickable body map links each system to its own records and flags.
  • The system is transparent by design: every alert traces back to its contributing readings.
  • Data are honestly labelled as measured, manual, derived, or simulated.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific grounding: NASA’s Human Research Program hazards guided the choice of indicators.
  • Connectivity: communication delay and intermittent links shaped the offline-first design.
  • Safety and honesty: ASTRA does not diagnose or replace a flight surgeon, uses fictional astronauts and synthetic data, and treats all thresholds as illustrative sample rules that need expert validation.
  • Privacy: authentication, role-based access, audit trails, and private well-being entries.
  • Usability: short check-ins, clear alert priorities, and non-alarming language to avoid overloading a busy crew.
  • Feasibility: a team-friendly stack and a phased plan that prioritises a working end-to-end demo.
